draft.title: Credit ratings and foreign confidence
card: A credit rating agency gives a government a grade for how likely it is to repay its debt on time. A top grade signals very low risk.
Foreign investors use ratings when deciding whether to lend. A lower rating signals more risk of not being repaid.
Lenders who see more risk can ask for a higher interest rate. So a lower rating can raise borrowing costs for the government and for banks and firms that borrow from overseas.
Lower confidence can also reduce demand for the country's assets and currency. This can weaken the dollar.
draft.remember: A lower rating signals more risk, which can lift borrowing costs and weaken the dollar.

a.q: What does a credit rating for a government show?
opts: How likely it is to repay its debt
How fast its economy is growing
How high its tax rates are set
How large its exports are each year
a.why: A credit rating grades the risk that a government will not repay what it owes. Growth and exports can affect the rating, but they are not what it measures, so those options are wrong.

b.q: An agency lowers the rating of Country Y. What is a likely result?
opts: Lenders ask for higher rates and its currency may weaken
Lenders ask for lower rates as the debt looks safer
Its currency may strengthen as demand for its assets rises
Its borrowing costs stay the same as lenders ignore ratings
b.why: A lower rating signals more risk, so lenders can ask for higher interest rates and may buy fewer of the country's assets, which can weaken the currency. Lower rates would suit a rise in the rating, so that option reverses cause and effect.
b.clue: More risk for a lender means a higher price for lending.

a.best: How likely it is to repay its debt

b.best: Lenders ask for higher rates and its currency may weaken

problems.detail: The clue 'The rating is about debt' gives the answer away. Only one option mentions debt, so a student can pick it without knowing the idea.

Why (b) says the lower-rates option 'reverses cause and effect'. It actually reverses the direction of the effect: lower rates would follow a higher rating, not a lower one. Better wording would be 'gets the direction wrong'.

check.summary: The facts are correct and both questions have one clear answer. The clue for (a) gives the answer away, and why (b) wrongly calls the reversed-direction option a reversal of cause and effect.
